essays.stem: Describe, step by step, how to measure the voltage across a lamp in a 12 V DC training circuit using a digital multimeter.
essays.modelAnswer: First I check the multimeter and its leads for cracks or damage, and make sure the meter has a CAT rating suitable for the work. I put the black lead in the COM socket and the red lead in the V Ω socket. I turn the dial to DC volts and choose a range higher than 12 V, such as 20 V, if the meter is not auto-ranging. With the circuit switched on, I hold the probes behind the finger guards and touch the black probe to the negative side of the lamp and the red probe to the positive side, so the meter is in parallel with the lamp. I read the display when it is steady. If it shows a minus sign, the probes are the wrong way round. I write down the reading with its unit, remove the probes, and switch the meter off.
markingPoints: Checks the meter and leads before use
Black lead in COM, red lead in V Ω socket
Selects DC volts and a range above the expected value
Connects the meter in parallel across the lamp, holding probes behind the finger guards
Reads when steady, records the value with its unit, and switches the meter off

essays.stem: Explain how to measure the current flowing through a lamp in a 12 V DC training circuit with a multimeter.
essays.modelAnswer: Current is measured with the meter in series, so that all the current flows through the meter. First I switch off the circuit. I set the meter to DC amps and move the red lead to the correct current socket: the 10 A socket if I am not sure how large the current is, and the black lead stays in COM. I open the circuit at one point, for example by taking one wire off the lamp terminal. I connect the red probe to the side coming from the positive of the supply and the black probe to the lamp, so that the meter fills the gap. I switch the circuit on and read the current. If the reading is very small, I switch off and move to a lower range. Afterwards I switch off, remove the meter, reconnect the wire, and put the red lead back in the V Ω socket so the meter is not damaged next time.
markingPoints: States that an ammeter is connected in series
Switches off before breaking into the circuit
Selects DC amps and the correct current socket, starting with the highest range
Opens the circuit and connects the meter into the gap, then switches on and reads
Switches off, reconnects the circuit and returns the red lead to the voltage socket

essays.stem: Describe how to measure the resistance of a resistor or a length of conductor, and explain why the circuit must be dead.
essays.modelAnswer: Resistance is measured with no voltage present, because the meter uses its own battery to pass a small current through the part. Any outside voltage could damage the meter and would give a false reading. So I isolate the circuit and prove it dead, or I take the part out of the circuit. I put the black lead in COM and the red lead in V Ω, and set the dial to ohms. I touch the probes together to check the leads: a digital meter should show close to zero, and on an analogue meter I use the zero adjust knob to set the needle to zero. I then hold the probes on each end of the resistor or conductor, keeping my fingers off the metal tips so my body does not change the reading. I read the value, check the unit (Ω, kΩ or MΩ), and compare it with what I expected.
markingPoints: Explains that the meter uses its own battery and that outside voltage would damage it or give a false reading
Isolates and proves the circuit dead, or removes the part
Sets the meter to ohms with the leads in the right sockets
Checks or zeroes the leads by touching the probes together
Holds the probes on each end without touching the tips, reads the value and unit and compares it

essays.stem: Explain what an insulation resistance test is for and describe how it is carried out on a dead circuit.
essays.modelAnswer: An insulation resistance test checks that the insulation between conductors, and between each conductor and earth, is in good condition, so that current cannot leak through it. Damaged insulation can cause shocks, fires and tripping. The tester makes its own high DC test voltage, so the circuit must first be isolated, locked off and proved dead. All lamps are removed and appliances are unplugged, and anything that could be damaged by the test voltage is disconnected. I check the tester and its leads, set it to the test voltage the instructor gives for the circuit, and test it with the leads joined and then apart. I then test between line and neutral, line and earth, and neutral and earth. Nobody may touch the conductors during the test. A good result is a high reading in megohms. Afterwards I let the circuit discharge, record the results and reconnect the lamps and appliances.
markingPoints: Says the test checks insulation between conductors and to earth, so current cannot leak
Isolates, locks off and proves the circuit dead first
Removes lamps, unplugs appliances and disconnects sensitive equipment
Tests between all conductors at the set voltage, keeping hands off the conductors
A good result is a high reading in megohms; lets the circuit discharge and records the results

essays.stem: Compare an analogue (needle) multimeter with a digital multimeter, giving the good and bad points of each.
essays.modelAnswer: An analogue multimeter has a needle that moves over a printed scale. Its good points are that you can see a reading rising or falling, which helps when a value is changing, and the needle shows a rough reading at a glance. Its bad points are that it is harder to read, because there are several scales, it can give a parallax error if you look from the side, it must be zeroed before measuring resistance, and it can be damaged by being dropped. A digital multimeter shows the reading as numbers on a display. It is easier and quicker for a beginner to read, it is usually more accurate, many models choose the range by themselves, and it shows a minus sign if the leads are reversed. Its bad points are that it needs a battery, a changing value can make the numbers jump about, and it can be harder to see a slow trend.
markingPoints: Describes the analogue meter: needle and scale; good for showing changing values
Analogue drawbacks: several scales, parallax error, needs zeroing, easily damaged
Describes the digital meter: numbers on a display, easy to read, usually more accurate
Digital advantages such as auto-ranging and showing reversed polarity
Digital drawbacks: needs a battery, jumping numbers, harder to see a trend

essays.stem: Explain how a clamp meter measures current, how to use one correctly, and why it is useful.
essays.modelAnswer: A clamp meter measures current by sensing the magnetic field around a conductor that is carrying current, so it does not need to be connected into the circuit. To use it, I check the meter and jaws for damage and set the dial to AC amps for a mains circuit. I open the jaws and close them around one single conductor, such as the line conductor, not the whole cable. If both line and neutral are inside the jaws, their equal and opposite currents cancel and the meter reads close to zero. I keep the jaws fully closed and read the display. A clamp meter is useful because the circuit does not have to be switched off or broken, which saves time and avoids disturbing connections. It is often used to check whether a circuit is overloaded or how much current a motor draws. At the Centre, clamp readings are taken only on equipment the instructor has set up for it, and no bare parts are ever touched.
markingPoints: Senses the magnetic field around a current-carrying conductor
Sets the correct current function (AC amps for mains)
Clamps around one conductor only, and explains why the whole cable reads near zero
Jaws fully closed; reads the display
Useful because the circuit is not broken; for example checking overload or motor current

essays.stem: Describe the safety precautions you should take when using electrical measuring instruments.
essays.modelAnswer: I use only instruments that are suitable for the job and have a CAT rating and voltage rating high enough for the place where I am measuring. Before use I check the meter case, the leads and the probes for cracks, bare metal or damage, and I use probes with shrouded tips and finger guards. I check that the meter's fuses are the type the maker states. I set the correct function and range before touching the probes to the circuit, and I never change the dial while the probes are connected. I hold the probes behind the finger guards and keep one hand away from the circuit where I can. Resistance, continuity and insulation tests are only done on circuits that are isolated and proved dead. I do not use meters in wet conditions. After use I switch the meter off and put the leads away. I follow the maker's instructions and the Centre's rules.
markingPoints: Chooses an instrument with a suitable CAT and voltage rating
Checks the case, leads and probes before use; uses shrouded probes with finger guards
Sets function and range before connecting; does not change the dial while connected
Holds probes behind the guards; resistance, continuity and insulation tests only on dead circuits
Avoids wet conditions; switches off and stores after use; follows the maker's instructions

essays.stem: Explain how measuring instruments should be cared for, stored and calibrated, and why this matters.
essays.modelAnswer: Measuring instruments must be looked after so that their readings stay accurate and they stay safe to use. I keep meters clean and dry and wipe them with a dry cloth after use, and I do not drop them or leave them where they can be knocked. I switch them off after use to save the battery, and replace the battery when the low-battery sign shows, because a weak battery can give wrong readings. I store each meter in its case with the leads coiled loosely, in a cool, dry place, away from heavy tools and out of hot vehicles. If a fuse blows, it is replaced only with the type the maker states. Instruments are sent for calibration at set times, where they are checked against an accurate standard and adjusted. The calibration date is recorded on a label. A meter that has been dropped, damaged or is out of date is taken out of use until it has been checked.
markingPoints: Explains that care keeps readings accurate and the meter safe
Keeps meters clean, dry and protected from knocks
Switches off after use and replaces low batteries
Stores in a case with leads coiled, away from heat and heavy tools
Calibration at set times against a standard, with the date recorded; damaged or out-of-date meters taken out of use

essays.stem: Explain Ohm's law and show how you could use it to check your measurements on a 12 V lamp circuit where the meter shows a current of 0.5 A.
essays.modelAnswer: Ohm's law says that the current in a circuit is equal to the voltage divided by the resistance, written I = V ÷ R. It can also be written V = I × R, or R = V ÷ I. If the voltage goes up and the resistance stays the same, the current goes up. In the lamp circuit, the supply is 12 V and the meter shows 0.5 A. Using R = V ÷ I, the resistance of the lamp while it is lit is 12 ÷ 0.5 = 24 Ω. I could check this by working out the lamp's power: P = V × I = 12 × 0.5 = 6 W. If the lamp is marked 12 V 6 W, my readings agree with its rating. If the numbers did not agree, I would check my meter settings, the connections and the supply voltage before trusting the result. A lamp's resistance is lower when it is cold, so a resistance reading taken with the circuit dead will be less than 24 Ω.
markingPoints: States Ohm's law correctly: I = V ÷ R, or V = I × R, or R = V ÷ I
Calculates the resistance correctly: 12 ÷ 0.5 = 24 Ω
Uses P = V × I to find the power (6 W) and compares it with the lamp's rating
Says what to check if the results do not agree
Notes that a cold lamp has a lower resistance than a lit one (or another sensible point about accuracy)

essays.stem: Explain how test results should be recorded, and what you should do if a reading is not what you expected.
essays.modelAnswer: Test results should be written on the proper test sheet or record straight after each measurement, so that they are not forgotten or mixed up. Each result should show what was tested and where, for example which circuit and between which conductors, the value with its unit, the instrument used and its range, the date and the name of the person who did the test. The writing must be clear and honest; a reading is never changed to make it look right. If a reading is not what I expected, I first check myself: are the leads in the right sockets, is the dial on the right function and range, and are the probes making good contact? I check the meter on a known value, such as a known resistor or a proving unit. I then measure again. If the reading is still wrong, I do not guess. I record what I found and report it to my supervisor, because it may show a fault.
markingPoints: Records straight after each test on the proper sheet
Shows what and where, the value and unit, the instrument, the date and the tester's name
Records honestly and never changes a reading
If unexpected, checks leads, function, range and contact, checks the meter on a known value, and measures again
Reports a confirmed unexpected reading to the supervisor as a possible fault

practical1.title: Measure voltage, current and resistance in series and parallel circuits on a 12 V DC training board
practical1.brief: As a group, build two simple circuits on the Centre's low-voltage training board and measure them with a digital multimeter: circuit A has two 12 V lamps (or two resistors given by the assessor) in series, and circuit B has the same two in parallel. The supply is a 12 V DC bench power supply or battery; no mains voltage is used. Every member makes at least one measurement of each kind while the others check the meter setting before it touches the circuit: (1) with the supply off, measure the resistance of each lamp or resistor and of the pair in series and in parallel, (2) with the supply on, measure the supply voltage and the voltage across each lamp, with the meter in parallel, (3) switch off, break into the circuit and measure the current with the meter in series, then switch on and read it. Record every reading in the group's results table with its unit, then use Ohm's law to work out what each reading should be and compare. Each member explains one result to the assessor. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical. Hand in the results table once for the whole group.
materials: Low-voltage training board with lamp holders or resistor terminals and connecting leads
12 V DC bench power supply or 12 V battery, with a switch or fuse in the circuit
Two 12 V lamps or two resistors given by the assessor
A digital multimeter with test leads in good condition
A results table sheet and a calculator
A phone or camera for the photos
photos: The meter and leads being checked, with the dial on the right setting
Resistance measured with the supply switched off
Voltage measured across one lamp in the series circuit, meter in parallel
The meter connected in series to measure current, with the leads in the current socket
The completed results table with measured and calculated values
The board taken apart and the meter switched off and stored
checklist: Checked the meter and leads before use
Chose the right function and range before connecting, and started high when the value was unknown
Measured resistance only with the supply switched off
Connected the meter in parallel for voltage and in series for current
Switched off before breaking into the circuit to measure current
Read the display correctly and recorded each value with its unit
Used Ohm's law to compare the measured and calculated values
Explained one result clearly to the assessor
Returned the red lead to the voltage socket, switched off the meter and stored it
safety: Use only the 12 V DC supply given; no mains voltage is used in this task
Never connect the meter across the supply while it is set to measure current
Lamps can get hot: let them cool before you touch them
Hold probes behind the finger guards; follow the maker's instructions and the Centre's rules

practical2.title: Continuity, insulation resistance and polarity tests on a dead lighting circuit, with a test record
practical2.brief: As a group, carry out dead tests on a simple lighting circuit (a one-way switch controlling a lamp holder) that is already wired on a practice board and is NOT connected to any supply. The assessor confirms that the board is disconnected, and the group proves it dead with a checked voltage tester before starting. Share the tests so that every member uses each instrument at least once, while the others check the setting and record the result: (1) check the continuity of each conductor end to end, and of the earth (protective) conductor to each metal part, with the low-resistance ohms or continuity setting, (2) check polarity: that the switch is in the line conductor and the lamp holder is connected the right way, (3) with the lamp removed and the switch on, carry out an insulation resistance test between line and neutral, line and earth, and neutral and earth, at the test voltage the instructor gives, keeping hands off the conductors during each test. Write every result on the Centre's test record sheet, with the instrument used. Each member explains one reading to the assessor. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical. Hand in the test record once for the whole group.
materials: Practice board with a wired one-way lighting circuit (switch, lamp holder and earth terminal), not connected to any supply
A two-pole voltage tester and its proving unit
A multimeter or low-resistance ohmmeter with a continuity setting
An insulation resistance tester with its leads
Short test leads with crocodile clips, for linking conductors where needed
A phone or camera for the photos
photos: The board shown disconnected, and proved dead with the tester checked on the proving unit
A continuity test on one conductor, with the meter display in view
The earth conductor continuity test to a metal box or fitting
The polarity check at the switch
The insulation resistance tester connected between two conductors, with the lamp removed
The instruments switched off and stored in their cases
checklist: Confirmed the board was disconnected and proved dead with a tester checked before and after
Checked each instrument and its leads before use
Zeroed or nulled the leads before measuring low resistance
Carried out the continuity tests correctly and read the values
Checked that the switch is in the line conductor
Removed the lamp before the insulation test and tested between all pairs of conductors
Kept hands off the conductors during the insulation test, and let the circuit discharge afterwards
Recorded each result, with its unit and the instrument used, on the test record
Explained one reading clearly to the assessor
safety: The board must not be connected to any supply; prove it dead before starting
The insulation tester makes its own high test voltage: never touch the conductors or probes during a test
Let the circuit discharge after each insulation test before you touch it
Use probes with finger guards and shrouded tips; follow the maker's instructions and the Centre's rules
